title: Nitrogen and sulfur
objectives: Explain the lack of reactivity of nitrogen in terms of its triple bond and lack of polarity
Describe the basicity of ammonia, the structure of the ammonium ion and its formation by an acid–base reaction
Describe the displacement of ammonia from ammonium salts by an acid–base reaction
State the natural and man-made occurrences of oxides of nitrogen and their catalytic removal from car exhaust gases
Explain why atmospheric oxides of nitrogen are pollutants, including their role in photochemical smog (PAN) and in the formation of acid rain
Describe the formation of atmospheric SO₃ from SO₂ and its role in acid rain, including the catalytic role of NO and NO₂
prior: Covalent and dative bonding, VSEPR shapes (Chapter 3)
Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases; the Haber process (Chapter 7)
why: Nitrogen makes up most of the air yet hardly reacts; ammonia, made from it, feeds billions of people as fertiliser. Car engines turn air into nitrogen oxides that cause smog and acid rain, and catalytic converters clean them up. These everyday applications are short but reliable marks in Papers 1 and 2.
intro: This chapter explains why nitrogen is so unreactive, describes ammonia and the ammonium ion as a base and its conjugate acid, and follows the oxides of nitrogen and sulfur through the atmosphere, from the car engine to acid rain and smog.

blocks.h: N₂ contains a triple bond (one σ and two π bonds) with a very high bond energy (944 kJ mol⁻¹), and the molecule is non-polar, so it does not attract electrophiles or nucleophiles. Reactions of N₂ need very high temperatures, lightning, or a catalyst.
Ammonia, NH₃, is pyramidal (107°) with a lone pair on nitrogen. The lone pair accepts a proton, so NH₃ is a Brønsted–Lowry base:
NH₃ is a weak base: only a small proportion reacts. With acids it forms ammonium salts: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl; 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.

items: The lone pair forms a dative bond to H⁺; then all four N–H bonds are identical.
NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral, 109.5° (four bonding pairs, no lone pair).
NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃: in water it is a weak acid, so ammonium salt solutions are slightly acidic.

blocks.h: Warming any ammonium salt with a base (NaOH, Ca(OH)₂, CaO) releases ammonia: an acid–base reaction (not redox). Test: the gas turns damp red litmus blue and has a pungent smell. Farmers should not add lime at the same time as ammonium fertilisers, because ammonia would be lost.

blocks.name: nh3game
blocks.title: Ammonia or not?
blocks.h: Decide whether each mixture gives off ammonia. Think about whether a base is present to remove H⁺ from NH₄⁺.

blocks.wrong: Heating an ammonium salt with acid releases ammonia.
blocks.right: An acid cannot take a proton from NH₄⁺. You need a base.

sections.title: Oxides of nitrogen and the atmosphere

head: source
how
rows: lightning supplies the energy for N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
high temperatures in car engines and power stations: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO; then 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂

head: problem
chemistry

NO₂ + unburnt hydrocarbons, in sunlight → PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate), an irritant

blocks.h: A honeycomb coated with platinum, rhodium and palladium (heterogeneous catalysts) converts the worst exhaust gases into harmless ones:

items: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂ (NO is reduced, CO is oxidised)

blocks.name: pollution
blocks.title: From engine to smog
blocks.h: Step through what happens to the gases from a car engine, from forming NO to acid rain, smog and the catalytic converter.

blocks.q: Why does a catalytic converter not reduce the amount of CO₂ released?
blocks.a: It produces CO₂ by oxidising CO and hydrocarbons. CO₂ is far less harmful locally than CO, NOₓ or hydrocarbons, but it is a greenhouse gas.

blocks.h: SO₂ comes from burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur, and from volcanoes. In the air it is slowly oxidised to SO₃, which dissolves in rain to form sulfuric acid. Nitrogen oxides catalyse the oxidation:

items: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO (NO₂ oxidises SO₂)
overall: SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃; then SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄

blocks.h: Acid rain damages buildings (especially limestone and marble), corrodes metals, lowers the pH of lakes (killing fish) and leaches nutrients from soil.

blocks.q: In SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO, what happens to the oxidation number of nitrogen?
blocks.why: NO₂ is reduced; it is the oxidising agent.

summary: N₂ is unreactive: very strong N≡N triple bond and no polarity.
NH₃ is pyramidal (107°) and a weak Brønsted–Lowry base: its lone pair accepts H⁺.
NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral (109.5°), with four identical N–H bonds; it is a weak acid.
NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O: warming an ammonium salt with a base releases ammonia (acid–base, not redox).
NO forms from N₂ and O₂ at high temperature (engines, lightning); NO is oxidised to NO₂ in air.
NO₂ → HNO₃ (acid rain); NO₂ + hydrocarbons + sunlight → PAN (smog).
Catalytic converters: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂; hydrocarbons oxidised to CO₂ + H₂O.
NO₂ catalyses SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃ (SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂); SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

assessment_s.q:
Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, is a fertiliser.
(a) Write an equation for its formation from ammonia and nitric acid and state the role of ammonia. [2]
(b) Describe a test to show the presence of NH₄⁺ in the fertiliser, with the equation. [3]
(c) Explain why NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral while NH₃ is pyramidal. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃; ammonia acts as a base (proton acceptor)
(b) warm with NaOH(aq); NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O; gas turns damp red litmus blue
(c) NH₄⁺: four bonding pairs, repel equally → tetrahedral 109.5°; NH₃: three bonding pairs + one lone pair, which repels more → pyramidal 107°

assessment_s.q:
Car exhausts contain NO, CO and unburnt hydrocarbons.
(a) Explain how NO is formed in the engine. [2]
(b) Give two harmful effects of nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere, with an equation for one. [3]
(c) Write an equation for one reaction in a catalytic converter and state which species is reduced. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) the very high temperature in the engine provides the energy to break the N≡N bond: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
(b) acid rain: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃; photochemical smog: NO₂ + hydrocarbons → PAN; catalyses SO₂ → SO₃
(c) 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂; NO is reduced

pp.skill: Why nitrogen is unreactive
pp.stem: Which statement explains why nitrogen gas is very unreactive?
opts: N₂ molecules have strong pd-pd forces between them.
The N≡N triple bond has a very high bond energy and the molecule is non-polar.
Nitrogen atoms have a full outer shell.
pp.exp: Breaking N≡N needs 944 kJ mol⁻¹, so reactions have a very high activation energy. The non-polar molecule also does not attract electrophiles or nucleophiles. Each N has a lone pair.

pp.skill: Counting bonding and non-bonding electrons
pp.mis: Counting lone pairs as single electrons
pp.stem: Which row is correct for the outer-shell electrons of all the atoms in the species?
pp.exp: NH₃: three N–H pairs (6 electrons) and one lone pair (2). N₂ has 6 bonding and 4 non-bonding (one lone pair on each N); NH₄⁺ has no lone pair; H₂O has two lone pairs (4).

pp.skill: Shape and bonding of the ammonium ion
pp.mis: Thinking NH₄⁺ keeps the lone pair
pp.stem: Which statement about the ammonium ion is correct?
opts: It is tetrahedral with all four N–H bonds identical.
It has a lone pair on the nitrogen atom.
It reacts with dilute acids to release ammonia.
pp.exp: The N lone pair of NH₃ forms a dative bond to H⁺; once formed, all four N–H bonds are the same (109.5°). NH₄⁺ is a weak acid, and NH₃ is released by alkalis, not acids.

pp.skill: Changes when ammonia forms an ammonium ion
pp.mis: Thinking the number of electrons around N increases
pp.stem:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen chloride: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl. Three statements:
1 A dative covalent bond forms.
2 The number of electrons in the outer shell of nitrogen increases.
3 The shape around nitrogen changes from pyramidal to tetrahedral.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: N already has 8 outer electrons in NH₃ (3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair); the lone pair becomes a bonding pair, still 8. The angle opens from 107° to 109.5°.

pp.skill: Ammonia and ammonium as base and acid
pp.mis: Saying ammonia bonds to hydroxide ions
pp.stem:
Three statements:
1 An NH₃ molecule uses its lone pair to accept a proton.
2 The ammonium ion is a Brønsted–Lowry base.
3 The H–N–H angle in NH₃ is smaller than in NH₄⁺.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: NH₃ is a base (proton acceptor). NH₄⁺ is its conjugate acid. Pyramidal NH₃ is 107°; tetrahedral NH₄⁺ is 109.5°.

pp.skill: Analysing the reaction of ammonia with water
pp.stem:
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
1 Water acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
2 Nitrogen is oxidised.
3 The H–N–H bond angle increases from NH₃ to NH₄⁺.
4 NH₄⁺ is the conjugate base of NH₃.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: Water donates H⁺ to NH₃. N stays −3 (not redox). Angle 107° → 109.5°. NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃.

pp.skill: Is forming ammonium a redox reaction?
pp.mis: Thinking any new bond means redox
pp.stem:
Ammonia dissolves in water, forming some NH₄⁺ ions.
1 This is a redox reaction.
2 The H–N–H bond angle increases as NH₄⁺ forms.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: No oxidation numbers change (N −3, H +1, O −2): acid–base only. The angle increases from 107° to 109.5°.

pp.skill: Correct statements about nitrogen compounds
pp.mis: Thinking N₂ has a double bond
pp.stem: Which statement is correct?
opts: Nitrogen is unreactive because of strong id-id forces between N₂ molecules.
Aqueous ammonium chloride is slightly acidic because NH₄⁺ donates protons to water.
High temperatures are needed to break the N=N double bond.
Sulfur dioxide reacts with unburnt hydrocarbons to form PAN.
pp.exp: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺, so NH₄Cl(aq) is about pH 5. N₂ has a triple bond; its unreactivity comes from bond strength, not intermolecular forces; PAN comes from NO₂.

pp.skill: Releasing ammonia from an ammonium salt
pp.stem: Which reagent, when warmed with ammonium chloride, releases ammonia?
pp.exp: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. Any alkali (or basic oxide) displaces ammonia from an ammonium salt.

pp.skill: Which mixtures produce ammonia
pp.mis: Expecting an acid to release ammonia
pp.stem:
Four mixtures are warmed.
1 NH₄NO₃(aq) and KOH(aq)
2 (NH₄)₂SO₄(s) and CaO(s) with a little water
3 NH₄Cl(aq) and dilute H₂SO₄
4 NH₄Cl(aq) and NaNO₃(aq)
Which produce ammonia?
pp.exp: Ammonia is released only when a base (OH⁻ from KOH or from CaO + water) takes H⁺ from NH₄⁺. Acids and neutral salts do not.

pp.skill: Role of hydroxide when ammonia is released
pp.stem: Ammonium sulfate is warmed with sodium hydroxide solution. What is the role of the hydroxide ions?
pp.exp: OH⁻ accepts a proton from NH₄⁺ (which acts as the acid): NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O.

pp.skill: Statements about releasing ammonia
pp.mis: Calling the ammonium ion a base
pp.stem:
Ammonium chloride is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
1 The ammonium ion acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
2 The oxidation number of nitrogen changes.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: NH₄⁺ donates H⁺ to OH⁻. N is −3 in both NH₄⁺ and NH₃: no redox.

pp.skill: Bond angle change when ammonia is released
pp.mis: Getting the direction of the angle change wrong
pp.stem:
Ammonium nitrate is warmed with aqueous potassium hydroxide.
1 Ammonia gas is given off.
2 The H–N–H bond angle increases as the reaction happens.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: NH₄⁺ (109.5°) becomes NH₃ (107°): the angle decreases, because the new lone pair repels more strongly.

pp.skill: Identifying the ammonium ion in a double salt
pp.stem: A blue crystalline double salt contains Cu²⁺ and one other cation. When it is warmed with NaOH(aq), a blue precipitate forms and a pungent gas turns damp red litmus blue. What is the other cation?
pp.exp: An alkaline gas released by warming with NaOH is ammonia, so the salt contains NH₄⁺. (The blue precipitate is Cu(OH)₂.)

pp.skill: Following a sequence of reactions of nitrogen compounds
pp.stem: An ammonium salt is warmed with an alkali, giving gas 1. Gas 1 is passed into dilute nitric acid, giving salt 2. What are gas 1 and salt 2?
pp.exp: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ (gas 1). NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃ (salt 2).

pp.skill: Reactions that produce a basic, soluble gas
pp.mis: Thinking NO₂ or SO₂ is basic
pp.stem:
Which reactions produce a basic gas that is very soluble in water?
1 NH₄Cl(s) heated with Ca(OH)₂(s)
2 N₂ + 3H₂ over an iron catalyst
3 copper with concentrated HNO₃
4 sulfur burned in air
pp.exp: Reactions 1 and 2 produce ammonia, the only common basic gas. Reaction 3 gives NO₂ and reaction 4 gives SO₂: both acidic.

pp.skill: Redox in the decomposition of ammonium nitrate
pp.mis: Thinking only one nitrogen atom changes
pp.stem: Ammonium nitrate decomposes on gentle heating: NH₄NO₃ → N₂O + 2H₂O. Which statement is correct?
opts: Nitrogen goes from −3 to +1 and from +5 to +1.
Only the nitrogen in NH₄⁺ changes oxidation number.
This is an acid–base reaction, not redox.
pp.exp: N in NH₄⁺ is −3 and in NO₃⁻ is +5; both end at +1 in N₂O. One N is oxidised and one reduced (the reverse of disproportionation).

pp.skill: Where NO comes from
pp.mis: Thinking NO is formed in the catalytic converter
pp.stem: Which statement about nitrogen monoxide, NO, is correct?
opts: It is formed in car engines when N₂ and O₂ react at high temperature.
It is formed in catalytic converters from NO₂.
It is a component of PAN formed from SO₂.
It dissolves in water to give a strongly alkaline solution.
pp.exp: The very high temperature in the engine supplies enough energy for N₂ + O₂ → 2NO. NO is also made naturally by lightning.

pp.skill: Roles of NO₂ in pollution
pp.mis: Thinking NO₂ is involved in only one problem
pp.stem: In which processes is nitrogen dioxide, NO₂, involved?
opts: both photochemical smog and acid rain
pp.exp: NO₂ reacts with unburnt hydrocarbons in sunlight to form PAN (smog), and with O₂ and water to form HNO₃ (acid rain). It also catalyses the oxidation of SO₂.

pp.skill: Statements about nitrogen oxides as pollutants
pp.stem:
Three statements:
1 NO is formed in engines from atmospheric N₂ and O₂.
2 NO₂ reacts with carbon monoxide to form photochemical smog.
3 NO₂, oxygen and water form nitric acid in acid rain.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: Smog (PAN) forms from NO₂ and unburnt hydrocarbons, not CO. 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃.

pp.skill: The pollutant that forms PAN
pp.stem: Which pollutant reacts with unburnt hydrocarbons in sunlight to form peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)?
pp.exp: PAN contains a nitrate group from NO₂. It is an eye irritant in photochemical smog.

pp.skill: Pollutants that react together in a catalytic converter
pp.stem: Which two pollutants react with each other on the surface of a catalytic converter?
pp.exp: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂: NO is reduced and CO is oxidised at the same time.

pp.skill: Removing hydrocarbons in a catalytic converter
pp.stem: Which reaction removes unburnt octane in a catalytic converter?
pp.exp: Unburnt hydrocarbons are oxidised completely to CO₂ and H₂O on the hot catalyst (Pt/Rh/Pd).

pp.skill: What is oxidised in a catalytic converter
pp.stem: Which pollutants are oxidised on the surface of a catalytic converter?
pp.exp: CO → CO₂ and CₓHᵧ → CO₂ + H₂O are oxidations. NOₓ are reduced to N₂.

pp.skill: Identifying a pollutant removed by a catalytic converter
pp.stem: Gas Y is colourless, odourless and very toxic because it binds to haemoglobin. It is removed by a catalytic converter. What is Y?
pp.exp: CO is toxic and is oxidised to CO₂ in the converter. NO₂ is brown; CO₂ is not removed (it is produced).

pp.skill: Changes in exhaust gas amounts across a converter
pp.stem:
Exhaust gases are analysed before and after a catalytic converter.
1 The amount of CO₂ increases.
2 The amount of N₂ increases.
3 The amount of NOₓ increases.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: CO and hydrocarbons are oxidised to CO₂; NOₓ is reduced to N₂, so NOₓ decreases.

pp.skill: Masses of products in a catalytic converter
pp.mis: Halving instead of keeping the N₂ ratio
pp.stem: What forms when 90 g of NO reacts completely with an excess of CO in a catalytic converter?
pp.exp: n(NO) = 90/30 = 3.0 mol. 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂: 3.0 mol CO₂ (132 g) and 1.5 mol N₂ (42 g).

pp.skill: Product volume with a limiting reactant
pp.stem: 6.0 g of NO reacts with 4.2 g of CO in a catalytic converter: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂. What is the total volume of N₂ and CO₂ formed, at room conditions?
pp.exp: n(NO) = 0.20, n(CO) = 0.15: CO is limiting. CO₂ = 0.15 mol, N₂ = 0.075 mol; total 0.225 mol × 24.0 = 5.4 dm³.

wrong.C: included the 0.05 mol of unreacted NO
wrong.D: used NO as the limiting reactant

pp.skill: The catalytic role of nitrogen oxides in acid rain
pp.stem:
Atmospheric SO₂ is converted to sulfuric acid.
step 1: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO
step 2: NO + ½O₂ → NO₂
step 3: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄
Which species acts as a catalyst?
pp.exp: NO₂ is used in step 1 and regenerated in step 2, so it is not used up overall: SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃.

pp.skill: Which species is reduced when SO₂ is oxidised
pp.stem: In the reaction SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO, which species is reduced?
pp.exp: N goes from +4 (NO₂) to +2 (NO): reduced. S goes from +4 to +6: SO₂ is oxidised by NO₂.

pp.skill: Whether NO or NO₂ can lead to SO₃
pp.stem: Sulfur is burned in excess oxygen. In experiment 1, NO is added to the gas mixture; in experiment 2, NO₂ is added. In which experiments can some SO₃ form?
pp.exp: NO is oxidised by the excess O₂ to NO₂, which then oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ (and is regenerated). So either oxide works as the catalyst.

pp.skill: Bonding and lack of reactivity of nitrogen; ammonia as a base
pp.stem: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air.

parts.q: Describe how a π bond is formed in the N₂ molecule.
ms: sideways overlap of p orbitals (one on each N)
electron density above and below the internuclear axis
the N≡N triple bond is very strong (high bond energy, 944 kJ mol⁻¹), so the activation energy for reactions is high

parts.q: Explain why ammonia acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base, and describe the change in shape when NH₄⁺ forms.
ms: the lone pair on N accepts a proton (H⁺)
four bonding pairs, no lone pair; all N–H bonds identical

pp.skill: Nitrogen oxides: sources, acid rain, smog and catalytic converters
pp.stem: Oxides of nitrogen, NOₓ, are important atmospheric pollutants.

parts.q: Give one natural and one man-made source of nitrogen oxides.
ms: man-made: internal combustion engines / power stations (high-temperature combustion)

Use equations to show the catalytic role of NO₂ in the oxidation of atmospheric SO₂.
State the main component of photochemical smog formed from NO₂ and how it forms.
ms: PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate), from NO₂ and unburnt hydrocarbons in sunlight
